sentences.text: This massive predator is estimated to have reached lengths between 11 and 12.2 meters with a weight ranging from 4 to 4.6 tons.
Known only from postcranial bones, it possessed a more slender build compared to other large theropods like Tyrannosaurus.
Richard Markgraf unearthed the fossils in April 1914 at Gebel Ghorabi near Ain Gedid, Egypt, before they were moved to Munich and formally described by Ernst Stromer in 1934.
The original specimens were destroyed during World War II bombings, though additional remains were later discovered in Agadez, Niger.
It inhabited the wetland environment of the Bahariya Formation alongside Tameryraptor and Spinosaurus.
If it is an abelisauroid, it may have been related to herbivorous or omnivorous taxa, suggesting minimal competition with carnivorous theropods.
Historically placed in Carcharodontosauridae and Tyrannosauroidea, its taxonomic position is now thought to belong in Noasauridae.
Some researchers hypothesize that Bahariasaurus is simply a juvenile version of Deltadromeus.
Bahariasaurus lived during the Cenomanian age of the Late Cretaceous in North Africa.
The fossil record for this animal spans from the Albian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 113.2 and 66 million years ago.
The attribution of fossils from Niger to Bahariasaurus is debated, with some researchers suggesting they belong to a carcharodontosaurid while others classify them as Theropoda incertae sedis.
